## SMS verification: What is it and how does it work?


Your password isn't protecting you anymore. In 2023 alone, hackers successfully breached accounts using stolen credentials[71% more often](https://www.ibm.com/reports/threat-intelligence) than the year before, while[over 24 billion](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/24-billion-credentials-circulate-dark-web-2022) username-password combinations were being sold on the dark web like baseball cards.


Ultimately, passwords are basically digital sticky notes at this point. LastPass finds that[62% of people](https://www.lastpass.com/resources/ebook/psychology-of-passwords-2022) reuse the same password (or slight variations) across multiple accounts. One breach, and suddenly your entire digital life is up for grabs.


That's where SMS verification comes in—and no, it's not just another annoying step between you and your account.


SMS verification adds a second layer of[security](https://www.twilio.com/docs/usage/security) by sending a verification code to your phone via text message. Even if hackers steal your password, they'd also need physical access to your phone to get in.


Unless they're really committed to ruining your Tuesday, that's a pretty effective deterrent.


The text verification process is simple:


1.


You enter your username and password


2.


Receive an SMS verification code on your phone


3.


Type in that code


And you're in. It takes about 30 seconds and dramatically reduces your chances of becoming another data breach statistic.


Whether you're a developer looking to add SMS verification to your app or a business owner trying to protect customer accounts, this guide covers everything you need to know about how SMS verification works, when to use it, and how to implement it without making your users want to throw their phones across the room.


## What is SMS verification?


SMS verification (also known as SMS two-factor authentication or SMS OTP) is a security method that confirms a user's identity by sending a temporary, single-use numeric code via text message to their mobile phone. Users enter this code into a website or app to prove phone ownership during account sign-up, login, or high-risk transactions.


SMS verification goes by other names too:


-


SMS authentication


-


SMS-based[two-factor authentication (2FA)](https://www.twilio.com/docs/glossary/what-is-two-factor-authentication-2fa)


-


SMS[one-time password (OTP)](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/blog/what-does-otp-mean)


SMS authentication to your mobile phone isn’t a silver bullet. There are still some security risks and costs to consider (which we cover below). However, its convenience and effectiveness make it a worthwhile approach for protecting your customers and their data. Plus, most modern consumers have gotten used to this kind of verification over the years since it doesn't require any additional apps or services.


## How does SMS verification work?


SMS verification is fairly straightforward. Here are the steps:


1.


Provide your phone number to a business during the account sign-up process (in addition to setting up a username and password).


2.


Enter your username and password on the business' website or app to receive a one-time text verification number.


3.


The site sends a one-time text verification (typically a six-digit code) to your phone number.


4.


Type that code into the app or website to complete the login process.


It's that straightforward. Give your phone number, get an SMS verification code, and sign on. This extra step of verification provides your account with significant additional protection from being hacked.


## SMS verification advantages


SMS verification remains the foundational layer for customer onboarding and account recovery because it balances security with near-zero user friction. SMS verification offers many benefits:


-


**Global reach (no app or smartphone required):** SMS works out of the box on virtually every mobile phone worldwide, including basic feature phones and regions with spotty mobile data.


-


**High onboarding conversion rates:** Every extra setup step during sign-up risks customer drop-off. Because SMS requires zero enrollment setup—and modern iOS and Android devices automatically autofill incoming one-time codes—users can verify their accounts in seconds without abandoning checkout or registration.


-


**Strong security:** SMS verification is still significantly more secure than a password alone, blocking the vast majority of automated credential-stuffing and bulk bot attacks.


-


**Familiarity and zero learning curve:** Many people are familiar with the process of entering a verification code received via SMS, making it a user-friendly option across every demographic and reducing customer support tickets for locked-out users.


-


**Affordability and fast deployment:** Implementing SMS 2FA is inexpensive compared to distributing physical hardware tokens or building custom push infrastructure. Users don’t need to install an app or get any additional hardware for their mobile phones, and developers can launch it in minutes using pre-built APIs.


## SMS verification challenges


While SMS verification blocks the vast majority of automated password attacks and offers unmatched global reach, scaling it safely requires protection against a few well-known telecom and fraud vectors. Rather than abandoning SMS, modern teams solve these challenges at the API layer:


-


**[SMS pumping](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/blog/sms-pumping-fraud-solutions) (Artificially Inflated Traffic):** Fraudsters use bots to trigger thousands of OTP requests to premium-rate numbers, driving up messaging bills. How to solve it: Use a verification service with automated traffic anomaly detection, such as[Twilio Verify Fraud Guard](https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify/preventing-toll-fraud/sms-fraud-guard) , which automatically blocks suspicious OTP spikes before messages are sent.


-


**[SIM swapping](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/blog/sim-swap-fraud) and port-out fraud:** Attackers can socially engineer a mobile carrier to transfer a user's phone number to a new SIM card or eSIM, intercepting incoming codes. How to solve it: Pair SMS verification with real-time carrier intelligence like[Twilio Lookup SIM Swap](https://www.twilio.com/docs/lookup/lookup-sim-swap) to flag recent SIM changes and trigger step-up authentication when a number looks risky.


-


**Phishing and real-time interception:** Because users manually type six-digit codes, sophisticated phishing sites can trick users into handing over an OTP in real time. How to solve it: Keep SMS for universal account recovery and low-friction onboarding, and layer in phishing-resistant channels like[Passkeys](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/blog/insights/best-practices/passkeys) or[Silent Network Auth (SNA)](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/blog/developers/best-practices/best-practices-sna) for high-value logins, all through a single API.


-


**Shared or lost devices:** If a user loses an unlocked phone or syncs text messages across a laptop and tablet, anyone with access to those screens could view incoming codes. How to solve it: Enforce short code expiration windows and mask sensitive previews where possible.


## Who uses SMS verification?


Companies from a wide range of industries—like banking,[healthcare](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/solutions/healthcare) social media, and retail—frequently use SMS verification to confirm a user’s identity. It's become a typical security feature found on both websites and mobile apps.


On the flip side, if you’re a consumer with an account for any of these services, then you're probably familiar with SMS verification. All it takes is receiving an SMS verification code and using it to sign in.


This method is popular because it's simple. It only requires a phone that can receive texts.


## Is SMS verification secure?


Yes, SMS verification is far safer than relying on a password alone, as it blocks automated credential-stuffing attacks, though it is less secure than phishing-resistant methods like passkeys or authenticator apps.


For hackers to compromise your account, they would typically need physical access to your phone (in addition to your username and password). Hackers could also try to transfer your number to a new phone if they get access to your personal information (such as your social security number).


If you want high-level security, we recommend using a solution like Verify. Verify lets you use other less-vulnerable verification methods, such as TOTP.

## How to choose a text verification service


With so many SMS text verification services, how do you find the right one for your business? Here are a few things to look for:


-


**Speed and reliability:** Look for a[service](https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/services) that delivers verification codes quickly and reliably, especially since users typically have only minutes to enter the code before it expires.


-


**Scalability:** If you’re sending thousands of SMS 2FA messages to customers, then you’ll need a service that can match your scale without sacrificing speed.


-


**Security:** SMS verification codes need to be secure. If not, attackers can intercept unprotected messages and use the code to gain access to your users’ accounts. Work with a verification service that's[SOC 2 compliant](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/topic/audit-assurance/audit-and-assurance-greater-than-soc-2) (the gold standard for data security).


-


**Top-notch support:** When something goes wrong, you need a service provider that can assist immediately.


-


**Alternate verification options:** Some users might not want to use their mobile phone for verification, and that's fine. Choose a provider with other 2FA options, such as email, push, or[TOTP](https://www.twilio.com/docs/glossary/totp) .

## SMS verification FAQs


### What if I haven't received my SMS verification code?


First, make sure that you have a strong cell phone signal—that's the most common culprit.


Next, confirm the website or app has the right phone number.


Lastly, ensure your mobile provider[isn't blocking messages from certain](https://support.twilio.com/hc/en-us/articles/4404317129627-Troubleshooting-undelivered-Authy-and-Verify-SMS-text-messages)[senders](https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/ui/sending-email/senders) or number types.


If those recommendations don't work, consider using an alternate verification method, such as voice, email, or TOTP.


### How do you bypass SMS verification?


Do you want to access a website or app but don't want to share your personal phone number? Set up a temporary phone number with Twilio—[it only takes about five minutes](https://www.twilio.com/blog/how-to-set-up-a-temporary-phone-number-in-less-than-five-minutes-with-twiml-bins-html) .


### How do you enable SMS authentication?


When setting up your account, you usually have the option to enable SMS as your preferred verification method. For existing accounts, check the security settings for your account.
